html:
cargo is the build system. Knowing its knobs is the difference between a two-minute build and a twelve-minute one.

Profiles

Profiles control optimisation. They are declared per package (or per workspace) and selected with a flag.

Rule of thumb: [profile.dev.package."*"] opt-level = 2 is the single best dev-experience tweak in Rust. Your code stays fast to recompile; dependencies (which never change) get optimised, so image decoding, regex and crypto stop being 20× slower than release.

LTO trade-off

lto Compile cost Speed
false baseline baseline
"thin" +10–20% +5–10%
"fat" / true +50–100% +10–15%

Measure before and after with cargo bench. Do not assume.

Build scripts (build.rs)

A build.rs at the package root runs before compilation. Uses: generating code, linking C libraries, embedding metadata.

Gotcha: if build.rs does not print cargo:rerun-if-changed, cargo re-runs it on every file change in the package. That is the usual cause of "why is my build script running constantly".

cargo subcommands worth knowing

Cross-compilation

Output lands in target/<triple>/release/. You need a linker for the target — usually a cross toolchain (gcc-aarch64-linux-gnu) configured in .cargo/config.toml:

Static binaries with musl — the reliable way to ship a Linux binary that runs anywhere:

cargo-zigbuild is a nicer alternative: it uses Zig as the cross linker and handles glibc version pinning for you.

Reducing build time

The usual culprits, in order of impact:

  1. [profile.dev.package."*"] opt-level = 2 — dependencies stop being slow.
  2. Fewer features. tokio = { features = ["full"] } compiles everything. List only what you need.
  3. sccache — shared compilation cache across branches and CI:
  4. Split into crates — unchanged crates are not recompiled.
  5. lld or mold as the linker. Linking is often 30–50% of build time:
  6. cargo-nextest for tests — parallel, per-test process isolation, much faster than cargo test on large suites.
  7. Check the tree. cargo tree -d and a look at cargo build --timings usually reveal one heavy dependency you can drop.

Lockfile hygiene

Duplicate major versions are normal and mostly harmless. They matter when:

  • the type appears in your public API (callers cannot interoperate),
  • a trait impl is missing because two serde versions exist,
  • binary size is critical.

.cargo/config.toml

Per-project cargo configuration. Commit it for repo-specific behaviour; keep machine-specific settings in ~/.cargo/config.toml.

A realistic CI build

--locked fails the build if Cargo.lock would change — that is what you want in CI, always.

Exercises

  1. Add [profile.dev.package."*"] opt-level = 2 to a project with image and regex. Time cargo run before and after.
  2. Write a build.rs that embeds the git commit hash as env!("GIT_HASH").
  3. Cross-compile a hello-world for x86_64-unknown-linux-musl and confirm with file that it is static.
  4. Run cargo build --timings and find the slowest crate. Is it one you need?
  5. Add [alias] entries so cargo t runs the full workspace test suite.
  6. Produce a release binary with lto = "fat", codegen-units = 1, panic = "abort", strip = true. Compare size and runtime against a default release build.
